questions.q: In Einstein's general relativity, what is gravity?
options: A force that reaches across empty space to pull two masses together
The curvature, or shape, of spacetime caused by mass and energy
A stream of particles exchanged between massive objects
The pressure of light pushing objects apart
questions.explanation: Einstein replaced Newton's force-at-a-distance with geometry: mass and energy bend the fabric of spacetime, and objects roll along the curves. As the episode puts it, matter tells spacetime how to curve, and curved spacetime tells matter how to move.

questions.q: What physically happens to space as a gravitational wave passes through a region?
options: Space heats up and glows in one direction
Space is stretched in one direction while squeezed in the perpendicular direction, then the two reverse
The objects in the region gain mass while the space stays fixed
All distances shrink uniformly in every direction at once
questions.explanation: A gravitational wave is a ripple in the shape of space. As it passes it stretches distances along one axis while squeezing the perpendicular axis, then reverses. It is the space between objects that changes, not the objects themselves.

questions.q: Why does LIGO rely on cosmic events like merging black holes rather than a source built in a laboratory?
options: Laboratories are not allowed to produce gravitational waves
Gravity is by far the weakest force, so only unimaginably heavy objects moving at enormous speeds make a detectable wave
Lab equipment moves too slowly to emit any waves at all
Gravitational waves can only form inside a vacuum, which labs lack
questions.explanation: Gravity is the weakest force in nature, with a tiny gravitational constant of about 6.67 x 10^-11. A detectable wave needs two black holes, each around 30 solar masses, orbiting hundreds of times a second. Nothing buildable comes within a trillion trillion times of that.

questions.q: A common objection is that a gravitational wave should stretch the laser's wavelength along with the arm, cancelling the effect. Why does LIGO still work?
options: The laser wavelength is fixed and immune to gravitational waves
LIGO measures the round-trip travel time of light and compares the two arms, which change in opposite directions, so a real difference remains
The mirrors absorb the stretched light before it returns
The wave affects the arm but never the light inside it
questions.explanation: LIGO is not laying a ruler against a table; it measures how long light takes for the round trip, which shows up as a phase shift, and it always compares the two perpendicular arms. While one arm lengthens the other shortens, so the differential signal is real and measurable.

questions.q: What is the key reason LIGO uses two detectors thousands of kilometres apart and only trusts coincident signals?
options: To take turns running so the equipment can rest
Local noise such as trucks and waves is local and never appears in both at once, but a real gravitational wave sweeps through both detectors
To make the laser beams twice as powerful
So one detector can serve as a spare if the other breaks
questions.explanation: Ground vibration is about a hundred billion times larger than the signal, but it is local: a truck near Livingston does not shake Hanford. A genuine gravitational wave crosses the whole planet, so the rule is to believe a signal only if both detectors see the same thing within the few milliseconds light takes to travel between them.

questions.q: Why does an inspiralling pair produce a chirp, a signal that rises in both frequency and amplitude?
options: The detector electronics add an artificial rising tone
As the orbit radiates energy as gravitational waves, the objects fall closer and orbit faster, so the wave rises in both pitch and amplitude until merger
The black holes are moving away from Earth, raising their pitch
The laser slowly increases in power during the measurement
questions.explanation: Radiating gravitational waves makes the orbit lose energy, so the objects fall closer and must orbit faster, which radiates even more energy in a runaway feedback loop. The gravitational wave frequency is twice the orbital frequency, so frequency and amplitude both climb together into the characteristic chirp ending in the merger.

questions.q: From memory, in your own words: why are heavy elements such as gold thought to be forged in neutron star mergers rather than inside ordinary stars?
keyPoints: Iron sits at the peak of the binding-energy curve, so building elements heavier than iron requires energy input rather than releasing it, and even dying stars cannot fuse past iron.
Making elements heavier than iron needs rapid neutron capture, the r-process, which demands an extremely neutron-rich and violent environment.
A neutron star merger flings out the most neutron-rich matter in the universe, where the r-process runs riot and produces gold, platinum and other heavy elements (a kilonova).
questions.explanation: If you recalled the iron wall on the binding-energy curve and linked the r-process to the neutron-rich debris of a merger, grade yourself Good or Easy. GW170817 confirmed this by showing a kilonova with the spectral fingerprint of strontium.

questions.q: From memory, in your own words: what made GW170817 the birth of multi-messenger astronomy, and what did the roughly 1.7 second gap between the gravitational waves and the gamma rays tell us?
keyPoints: It was detected first in gravitational waves, then 1.74 seconds later as a gamma-ray burst, and later in visible light, so one event was studied with both light and warped spacetime.
The gravitational waves came directly from the merger, while the gamma rays came from a jet that took a moment to form and punch out, explaining the short delay.

Arriving within about 2 seconds after travelling side by side for 130 million years showed gravity and light travel at the same speed to better than one part in a thousand trillion, ruling out whole families of rival theories.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that multiple messengers (gravitational waves, gamma rays, visible light) observed one event, and that the tiny delay confirmed gravity and light share the same speed, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: The two black holes in GW150914 had masses of about 36 and 29 solar masses, but the final merged black hole was about 62 solar masses. How many solar masses were radiated away as gravitational waves?
working: By \(E = mc^2\) this missing mass became the energy of the gravitational waves (around \(5 \times 10^{47}\) joules).
questions.explanation: The three missing solar masses did not go anywhere; they became the wave. Via Einstein's mass-energy equivalence E = mc^2, that mass was converted directly into the energy of gravitational waves, briefly radiating more power than every star in the visible universe combined.

questions.q: Why were the LIGO scientists, including Marco Drago, initially convinced the September 2015 signal was not real?
options: The two detectors disagreed completely with each other
LIGO secretly fed fake blind-injection signals into the data to keep scientists honest, and this signal looked so perfect they assumed it had been planted
The detectors were known to be broken at the time
Gravitational waves had already been ruled out by earlier experiments
questions.explanation: LIGO used blind injections, deliberately planted fake signals, to test whether the team could find and analyse a real event. The chirp was so clean and textbook that Drago assumed someone had injected it. Only after the four people authorised to know confirmed no injection had been made was it accepted as a real signal.

questions.q: Explain how the detection of GW150914 provided a confirmation of Einstein's general relativity. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Einstein's general relativity predicted gravitational waves: ripples in the curvature of spacetime emitted when very massive objects accelerate violently, travelling outward at the speed of light. In September 2015 LIGO directly detected such a wave, measuring arm-length changes of about 4 x 10^-18 metres, roughly a thousandth the width of a proton. The recorded waveform, including the inspiral, merger and ring-down, matched the waveform computed from Einstein's equations point for point, confirming the prediction almost exactly 100 years after the theory was written.

criteria.descriptor: States that general relativity predicted gravitational waves as ripples in spacetime travelling at the speed of light.
Identifies that LIGO directly detected such a wave, measuring an extraordinarily small change in arm length.
States that the measured waveform matched the prediction of Einstein's equations, confirming the theory.

questions.explanation: The marker rewards linking the theoretical prediction to the direct measurement and to the match between the recorded and predicted waveforms.
